`process.umask()` is [well-defined on Windows in Node.js](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#processumask) — it's not a no-op. Bun inherits this behavior. The permission assertion is guarded by `process.platform !== "win32"` because Windows doesn't use Unix permission bits, but the umask itself functions correctly on both platforms.

Wrapping the umask call in a platform guard would leave it unset on Windows, which is harmless today (since the assertion is skipped), but also means the test silently diverges in setup between platforms for no real benefit. The current approach is simpler and correct: set a known umask, run the test, restore — the platform guard handles the assertion side.

This step still references `matrix.settings.name`, but the job no longer defines a matrix. That will make the artifact name expression fail at runtime. Update the artifact name to a static value (e.g., `unit-linux-...`) or reintroduce the matrix.

This config file defines the `hooks` key twice. In JSON/JSONC, the later `hooks` object overwrites the earlier one, so the `guardrails.sh` hook will be ignored. Merge these into a single `hooks` object with both entries under `PreToolUse`.

The README links to `managed/opencode.json` using an absolute local filesystem path (`/Users/...`). This won’t work for other developers or in GitHub rendering. Use a repo-relative link (e.g., `./managed/opencode.json`).

`z.boolean().default(true).optional()` makes the outer schema optional, which can prevent the default from being applied (missing `notifications` may parse to `undefined` rather than `true`). If the intent is a default-true flag, prefer `z.boolean().optional().default(true)` or drop the trailing `.optional()`.

`detectRepetition(...)` is called on every `reasoning-delta` event after appending text. Because `detectRepetition` scans up to 197 pattern lengths over an 8KB window, this can become expensive during streaming and may impact responsiveness. Consider throttling (e.g., only check every N characters / once per second) or maintaining an incremental tail buffer to reduce repeated full scans.

`detectRepetition(...)` is also called on every `text-delta` update. This repeats the same potentially expensive scan during streaming output and can amplify CPU usage. Consider throttling or only checking when the text length crosses thresholds (e.g., every 256–1024 appended chars) to keep streaming lightweight.

`pull_request_target` + checking out the PR head SHA + running the test suite executes untrusted PR code in the base repo security context (with an authenticated `GITHUB_TOKEN`). For CI that runs code from PRs, prefer `pull_request` (or otherwise avoid executing the head revision under `pull_request_target`).

This workflow runs on `pull_request_target` and passes `OPENCODE_API_KEY` for PRs from non-team authors. Because `pull_request_target` exposes secrets to workflows, an untrusted contributor PR can trigger a run that has access to this secret. Consider restricting execution to non-fork PRs / trusted authors, or switching to `pull_request` and removing secret usage for external PRs.

The existing check (looking for `part.type === "compaction"` in the message parts) handles the **follow-up user message** that is created _after_ compaction — at that point the stored message already contains a `compaction`-typed part.  
But during the **compaction LLM call itself**, `incoming.message` is the in-flight request: the compaction message part hasn't been persisted to the session yet. Without the `incoming.agent === "compaction"` early return, `sdk.session.message()` would be called, find no `compaction` part, and the header would fall through to `"user"`.

The error handler drops the original caught error object (`err`) and only logs a derived message. This makes debugging harder (no stack/metadata). Consider including the original `err` in the log fields (or as `cause`) in addition to the user-facing message.
```suggestion
          log.error("failed to parse skill frontmatter", { skill: match, error: message, err })
```

For invalid frontmatter, the `message` is taken from only the first Zod issue. This often yields generic text like "Required" and loses which field failed and any additional issues. Consider formatting a clearer message (e.g., include issue `path` and/or join multiple issues) before logging/storing it.

`error: message` is persisted onto `Skill.Info` and returned by `Skill.all()` (and thus the `/skill` API). The message can include parser details and potentially snippets of the SKILL.md contents, which may be sensitive. Consider omitting `error` from the public API response, or sanitizing/shortening it (e.g., a generic code plus a verbose-only detail).

`Skill.all()` now returns invalid entries, but `Skill.get()` only looks in `s.skills` (valid skills). This makes it possible for consumers to see a skill name from `all()` that can never be retrieved via `get()`. Consider either filtering invalids out of `all()` (and adding a separate `invalid()` accessor) or extending `get()` to return invalid entries with `status: "invalid"`.

      disabled: skill.status === "invalid",

`disabled: true` options are filtered out by `DialogSelect` (it does `filter((x) => x.disabled !== true)`), so marking invalid skills as `disabled` will prevent them from being displayed at all. In `fmt(..., { verbose: true })` the new `<error>` tag embeds `skill.error` directly into XML-like output. This file defines "hooks" twice (first at line 121, again at line 133). In JSON/JSONC, duplicate keys are overridden by the later value, so the earlier PreToolUse hook for guardrails.sh will be silently dropped. Merge these into a single "hooks" object (one PreToolUse array containing all entries), or use separate events/arrays inside one hooks block.

Switching this workflow to `pull_request_target` is dangerous because the jobs execute PR code (via checkout of the PR head SHA) with a base-repo `GITHUB_TOKEN` that has `checks: write`. A malicious fork PR can exfiltrate the token and write to the repo/checks. Prefer `pull_request` for running tests on PR code, or keep `pull_request_target` only for non-executing metadata tasks and run code on `pull_request` with minimal permissions and no secrets.

Using `pull_request_target` here runs typechecking against the PR's head SHA in the base-repo security context. That executes untrusted code with elevated token access. Prefer `pull_request` for code-executing checks, or ensure the workflow checks out only trusted refs and sets explicit minimal `permissions:` to avoid exposing write-capable tokens to forked PR code.

`runHook()` hard-codes `Process.run(["sh", "-c", command], ...)`. This will fail on Windows where `sh` is typically unavailable, and it also constrains hooks to POSIX shells. Consider using `Process.run` with `shell: true` (so cross-spawn picks the platform shell), or branching on `process.platform` to use `cmd /c` on win32.

`detectRepetition()` is called on every `reasoning-delta` after appending text. The implementation scans 4..200 pattern lengths over an 8KB window, which can become expensive during streaming (many small deltas). Consider throttling checks (e.g., only after N chars appended / at most once per X ms) or moving to an incremental/tail-only heuristic to reduce per-delta CPU.

Same concern as above: `detectRepetition()` is invoked on every `text-delta` (streaming output). This can add significant CPU overhead in long responses. Throttle or make detection incremental so streaming updates don’t repeatedly rescan the full 8KB tail.

The unit job no longer defines a matrix, but the unit artifact upload step above still references `matrix.settings.name` in its `name:` field. That will break workflow evaluation. Update the artifact name to a constant (e.g. `unit-linux-${{ github.run_attempt }}`) or reintroduce the matrix.

`hooks` is declared twice in this JSONC object. In JSON/JSONC, the later key wins, so the `guardrails.sh` hook block is effectively dropped and only the factcheck hook remains active. Merge these into a single `hooks` object (e.g., combine both `PreToolUse` entries into one array) so both hooks are applied.

This schema chains `.default(true).optional()`. In Zod, applying `optional()` after `default()` makes the default ineffective (the field can remain `undefined`), which contradicts the intended default behavior described here. Prefer either `z.boolean().default(true)` or `z.boolean().optional().default(true)` (depending on the desired output type).

This link uses an absolute local filesystem path (`/Users/.../managed/opencode.json`), which will be broken for everyone else viewing the README. Use a repo-relative link (e.g., `managed/opencode.json`) so it works on GitHub and in other environments.

`pull_request_target` checks out and executes the PR’s code (`ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha`) while the workflow has elevated permissions (`checks: write`). For PRs from forks, this lets untrusted code run with the base-repo token/permissions and can be used to exfiltrate the `GITHUB_TOKEN` or tamper with checks. Prefer `pull_request` for running tests/typecheck on untrusted code, or significantly reduce permissions and avoid executing PR code in a `pull_request_target` workflow.
```suggestion
  pull_request:
```

Using `pull_request_target` while checking out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` and running `bun typecheck` executes untrusted PR code in the base-repo security context. Since this workflow doesn’t pin minimal `permissions`, the resulting `GITHUB_TOKEN` privileges can be higher than intended. Prefer `pull_request` for CI that runs PR code, or explicitly set minimal permissions and avoid running arbitrary PR code under `pull_request_target`.

The PR description/title focuses on guardrails fixes and tests, but this hunk introduces a new memory auto-extraction path in the core session processor (Config gating + background extraction/flush). Please update the PR description (or split the change) so reviewers can evaluate memory-system behavior, risk, and rollout implications explicitly.

These tests call `MemoryExtractor.track*()` and `cleanup()` but contain no assertions about the resulting side effects (e.g., that entries were persisted to the store or written to `.opencode/memory/`). As written, they can pass even if the extractor becomes a no-op. Add assertions by stubbing `MemoryStore.runPromise` / `MemoryFile` calls (or by reading back created files) so the tests fail when extraction behavior regresses.

`input_mode_normal` is defaulted to `escape`, but `session_interrupt` is also defaulted to `escape`. Because command keybind handling triggers the first matching enabled command, pressing Escape while in shell mode during a running session will match `session_interrupt` before this command, preventing the intended “Exit shell mode” behavior. Consider changing the default for `input_mode_normal`, or adjusting priority/enablement (e.g., disable `session_interrupt` when `store.mode === "shell"`, or register the shell-exit command before interrupt).

`input_mode_normal` defaults to `escape`, but `session_interrupt` also defaults to `escape` in this same keybind config. With both enabled in the prompt, Escape can become ambiguous and prevent exiting shell mode (or prevent interrupt) depending on command ordering. Consider picking a non-conflicting default for `input_mode_normal` (or documenting/handling the precedence explicitly).

The context-status threshold logic here diverges from the core overflow/compaction logic (e.g. `packages/opencode/src/session/overflow.ts`). In particular, treating `model.limit.context === 0` as a real limit will mark almost any session as “insufficient”, and the reserved/usable computation uses a hard-coded 32k cap instead of `ProviderTransform.maxOutputTokens(...)` / the shared `isOverflow(...)` helper. Recommend reusing the shared overflow calculation (and explicitly treating context=0 as “unknown/unlimited”) so the panel matches actual compaction behavior.

`status(val.model)` is computed twice during render, which repeats the token/threshold calculation and can lead to inconsistent output if the underlying reactive values change between calls. Compute it once (e.g., `const s = status(val.model)`) and reference `s.color`/`s.text`.

`req()` currently forwards an arbitrary set of headers provided by the frontend into the WebSocket handshake. Because `open_socket` is a privileged Tauri command, this effectively lets renderer code spoof sensitive handshake headers (e.g., `Host`, `Origin`, `Cookie`, `Sec-WebSocket-*`) and increases the impact of any renderer compromise (SSRF/auth header forwarding). Consider restricting this to an allowlist (likely just `Authorization` for this PR) and explicitly rejecting/ignoring disallowed names.

The helper function is named `drop`, which shadows Rust’s standard `drop` and makes call sites harder to read/grep. Renaming it to something like `remove_socket`/`remove_conn` (and updating call sites) would reduce confusion.
```suggestion
fn remove_socket(state: &Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, mpsc::UnboundedSender<SocketMsg>>>>, id: &str) {
```

`connect_async(req).await` has no timeout. If DNS/TCP/TLS negotiation stalls, the background task can hang indefinitely and the `SocketState` entry for `id` will never be removed (and `close_socket` can’t complete the shutdown). Consider wrapping the connect in `tokio::time::timeout` and calling `fail(...)` + removing the map entry on timeout.

The renderer-side socket drops the backend-provided error message (`evt.message`) and does not transition the socket to CLOSED on an `error` event. If the underlying `ws` implementation emits `error` without a subsequent `close`, consumers may remain stuck in CONNECTING/OPEN. Consider calling `fail(evt.message)` (or otherwise ensuring `readyState` becomes CLOSED and the message is surfaced somewhere) for parity with the Tauri implementation.
```suggestion
        fail(evt.message)
```

`detectLinks` is only wired into the main `TextPart` markdown `<code>` render path, but `ReasoningPart` also renders `filetype="markdown"` via `<code>` without `onChunks`. That means wrapped URLs inside the (non-experimental) thinking/reasoning markdown can still lack OSC 8 link metadata and break on visual wraps. Consider also passing `onChunks={detectLinks}` to the `<code filetype="markdown">` in `ReasoningPart` for consistency.

`notifications` is defined as `z.boolean().default(true).optional()`. In Zod, calling `.optional()` after `.default(...)` prevents the default from being applied when the field is omitted. To make the default effective, drop `.optional()` or place `.default(true)` last (after `.optional()`).

`process.chdir(process.env.OPENCODE_ORIGINAL_CWD)` can throw (e.g. directory deleted, permission issues, invalid value), which would crash the CLI very early. Wrap this in a try/catch (and possibly validate the path) so the bun fallback can't brick startup.

`writeIndex`/`writeEntry` write `.opencode/memory/.keep` and other files but never create the `.opencode/memory` directory first. `Bun.write()` does not create missing parent directories, so first-run memory writes will fail with ENOENT. Create the directory (e.g. `fs.promises.mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })`) before writing files.

The AppleScript example likely won't work as written: `display notification ...` is not a command supported by the Terminal application, so `tell application "Terminal" to display notification ...` typically errors. Use the plain `display notification ...` form (or tell `System Events`) so the docs example is executable.

This link is an absolute local filesystem path (`/Users/...`) which won't work for other developers or in the published package/docs. Use a relative repo link (e.g. `managed/opencode.json`) or a GitHub URL.

The upload-artifact name references `${{ matrix.settings.name }}`, but this job no longer defines a matrix. This will fail at runtime. Update the artifact name to a static value (e.g. `unit-linux-...`) or reintroduce the matrix.

Switching unit/e2e workflows to `pull_request_target` while checking out and executing the PR head SHA runs untrusted code with the base repo’s token permissions. Even with `contents: read`, this pattern is a common secret/token exfiltration vector. Prefer `pull_request` for running tests, or keep `pull_request_target` but only operate on the base SHA / avoid executing PR code (or aggressively restrict permissions and avoid any secrets).

Using `pull_request_target` here will execute `bun typecheck` from the PR’s codebase with the base repo token context. That’s risky for PRs from forks (untrusted code). Prefer `pull_request` for typechecking, or run a safe, non-executable check that doesn’t require checking out PR code under `pull_request_target`.

This workflow uses `pull_request_target`, checks out the PR head SHA, and has `pull-requests: write` plus uses `gh api/gh pr comment`. A malicious fork PR can modify repo files that the workflow executes/reads and potentially abuse the write token. To reduce risk, avoid checking out PR code under `pull_request_target` (use base SHA + GitHub API for diffs), or switch to `pull_request` with read-only permissions and no secrets.

Same concern here: `pull_request_target` + checkout of PR head SHA + `pull-requests: write` + `gh pr comment` executes against untrusted code. Consider generating the changed workflow file list via GitHub API without checking out PR code, or run this under `pull_request` with restricted permissions.

This workflow is triggered by `pull_request_target` (and also `check_suite`) and includes jobs with `pull-requests: write`. Be careful not to check out or execute untrusted PR code in any job under `pull_request_target`, and avoid using repository secrets for fork PRs—otherwise it becomes a token/secret exfiltration vector. If you need fork compatibility, prefer `pull_request` for test execution and reserve `pull_request_target` for minimal, non-code-executing metadata actions.

This looks like local tool state/telemetry (`.claude/state/*`) rather than source-controlled project content. Committing it will create noisy diffs and may leak local paths/session IDs. Consider removing these `.claude` state files from the PR and adding the directory (or at least `.claude/state/`) to `.gitignore`.

Same concern as other `.claude/state/*` additions: this is local runtime state and typically shouldn’t be committed to the repo. Please remove it from source control (and ignore it going forward) to avoid churn and accidental leakage of local metadata.

These tests mostly exercise the methods without asserting any observable behavior (they will pass even if the extractor stops recording anything). Add assertions against the expected persisted output/state (or explicit spies/mocks) so regressions are caught.

`runHook` always executes via `sh -c`. On Windows hosts this will typically fail (no `sh`), causing hooks to silently not run (caught and treated as pass). If hooks are expected to work cross-platform, consider using `Process.run(..., { shell: true })` or selecting an OS-appropriate shell (`cmd.exe`/PowerShell) so guardrails aren’t skipped on win32.

Same as English docs: `tell application "Terminal" to display notification ...` is unlikely to work because `display notification` isn’t a Terminal command. Please fix the AppleScript snippet here as well (and keep locales consistent).
